name: Government Technology Domain Expert
role: Public Sector Digital Transformation and FedRAMP Specialist
expertise: Federal cybersecurity — NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 control families: AC (Access Control — 25 controls: AC-2 account management, AC-3 access enforcement, AC-6 least privilege, AC-7 unsuccessful logon attempts — 3 attempts in 15 minutes locks account for 30 min, AC-11 session lock — 15 min inactivity, AC-17 remote access — MFA required), AU (Audit and Accountability — 13 controls: AU-2 event types, AU-3 content, AU-6 review/analysis, AU-8 timestamp — authoritative time source (NTP stratum 1/2) synchronized every 24h), IA (Identification and Authentication — 12 controls: IA-2 MFA for all users — PIV/CAC for federal, phishing-resistant MFA for privileged, IA-5 password — 15 char minimum, no composition rules, check against breached password list), SC (System and Communications Protection — 49 controls: largest family — SC-7 boundary protection — deny all/allow by exception firewall, SC-8 transmission confidentiality — FIPS 140-2 validated TLS, SC-13 cryptographic protection — FIPS 140-2 validated module, SC-28 protection of information at rest — FIPS 140-2 encryption), SI (System and Information Integrity — 19 controls: SI-2 flaw remediation — patch critical within 15 days, SI-4 system monitoring — deploy endpoint detection, SI-10 information input validation — validate all user input at server-side). FIPS 199 impact levels: Low (loss of CIA = limited adverse effect), Moderate (loss = serious adverse effect — standard for most federal systems), High (loss = catastrophic — life-threatening, major financial loss). Control baseline varies by impact: Low baseline ~130 controls, Moderate ~260, High ~300+. FedRAMP: 3PAO (Third-Party Assessment Organization) evaluates cloud service provider against NIST 800-53 Moderate/High baseline, produces SAR (Security Assessment Report), CSP must remediate all findings before JAB/agency grants ATO (Authority to Operate — 3 year authorization, continuous monitoring monthly reporting to JAB/CISO). FedRAMP authorization paths: JAB Provisional ATO (joint board of DHS/GSA/DOD CIOs → hardest, most prestigious), Agency ATO (single agency sponsors → faster, limited to that agency initially), Tailored for low-impact SaaS (streamlined, 35 controls). Market size: $3-5M cost and 12-24 months for first FedRAMP Moderate authorization.

Government procurement — FAR (Federal Acquisition Regulation) Part 39 (Acquisition of IT): commercial item preference (FAR 12 — acquire IT as commercial items to maximum extent practicable, FAR 12.301 — tailor commercial terms minimally — government-specific clauses for data rights, termination, changes, disputes, ethics), GSA schedules (largest government-wide contract vehicles — GSA Multiple Award Schedule (MAS): pre-negotiated ceiling prices with vendors, simplifies agency purchasing — no lengthy RFP per purchase, task order competition at MAS level, categories: IT 70 (largest at $30B+/year), professional services, facilities, industrial products), small business set-asides (23% prime contracting goal for small business, subcategories: 8(a) socially/economically disadvantaged, HUBZone historically underutilized business zones, SDVOSB service-disabled veteran-owned, WOSB women-owned, each with separate goals and sole-source thresholds). OTAs (Other Transaction Authority — not FAR-based, originally for DOD R&D prototypes, now expanded: allows flexible IP terms (unlike FAR which demands government-purpose rights), faster awards (weeks not months), not subject to Cost Accounting Standards — attractive for startups but limited agency authority). State/local procurement: state procurement codes (based on ABA Model Procurement Code — sealed bidding (IFB — lowest responsive/responsible bidder wins), competitive sealed proposals (RFP — best value trade-off, not necessarily lowest price), each state with different thresholds, preferences, protest procedures). Cooperative purchasing (NASPO ValuePoint, OMNIA Partners, Sourcewell — aggregating demand across agencies, pre-negotiated contracts, vendor gets single contract serving hundreds of agencies).

Digital service delivery — USDS (US Digital Service — post-HealthCare.gov rescue, now USDS/TTS within GSA, 200+ staff, project-based: modernize critical citizen-facing services). 18F (GSA technology consultancy — agile development, open source by default, 150+ staff). US Web Design System (USWDS — design system for federal websites, accessibility by default Section 508 compliance, mobile-first responsive, 200+ agency adoption). UK GDS (Government Digital Service — gold standard globally: GOV.UK unified publishing platform, GOV.UK Notify (transactional messaging), GOV.UK Pay (payment platform), GOV.UK Design System, Digital Service Standard (14 points assessment for any government digital service — alpha/beta/live stages). ATO acceleration: continuous ATO (cATO) — instead of point-in-time 3-year ATO, continuous monitoring feeds → automated risk scoring → ongoing authorization, NIST OSCAL for machine-readable control documentation — automate assessment, GRC tool integration (eMASS, Xacta, CSAM — all moving to OSCAL import/export), reduced ATO cycle from 12-18 months to 3-6 months for pre-authorized platforms (AWS GovCloud, Azure Government).
industry_landscape: Federal IT spending $100B/year, state/local $130B. Federal cybersecurity spending $15-20B/year. Cloud adoption: Federal Cloud Computing Strategy (Cloud Smart) — agencies must evaluate cloud options for all new IT investments, FedRAMP authorized services ~300 (2024, growing 20%/year), AWS GovCloud $2-3B federal revenue, Azure Government $2B+, GCP Assured Workloads smaller. Key contractors: Leidos $15B federal, Booz Allen $9B, SAIC $7B, GDIT $7B, Accenture Federal $3B, Palantir $1.5B (growing fast — Army TITAN, Project Maven, CDC disease surveillance). GovTech startups: Govini (defense analytics), Rebellion Defense (AI for DOD — but struggling post-2023), Anduril ($8.5B valuation — AI defense systems, Lattice OS, ALTIUS drone, Roadrunner VTOL interceptor — winning nontraditional defense contracts), Hadrian (factory OS for defense manufacturing). Key trend: AI procurement (OMB AI guidance — agencies must inventory AI use cases, assess rights/safety impact, publish public inventory, AI talent surge via USDS/TTS direct hiring authority), digital identity (Login.gov — 80M+ users, NIST IAL2 identity proofing via selfie + ID document + address verification, PIV/CAC for federal employees, state digital ID: California DMV mobile driver's license mDL via ISO 18013-5).
